A Warning About Conceptual Science

Aug 10, 2016 • Janice Cotcher

Scientific jargon can often mask a lack of understanding. A scientifically literate person is not the one with “a command of the most names, but the one who knows which he understands and which he doesn’t.”[2] Consider the example of capillarity:

Similarly, there are those who say that the reason water climbs up thin hollow tubes is because of capillarity. Again this is not true. When water climbs up thin narrow tubes it is because of electrical forces - the attractive forces between the water molecules and the molecules that make up the inner wall of the tube are greater than the attractive forces between the water molecules themselves. Capillarity is the name given to this climbing behavior of liquids, not the reason for it. [2]

The Biological Sciences Curriculum Study (BSCS) 5E Learning Model (Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, and Evaluate) is perhaps the most popular and widely used in the classroom. To assess that all students are progressing adequately through the early phases of the cycle, E. Duran et al. recently suggest modifying the 5E model to add a conscious pause called the Express phase. An active formative assessment of learning after the Explain phase, the Express phase allows students to express their ideas about the learning that has occurred at this point in the learning cycle. The teacher can assess whether misconceptions identified during the Engage phase have been corrected during the Explore and Explain phases and if additional Explore and Explain phases are needed. In that regard, the Express phase allows teachers to analyze and assess their own teaching effectiveness. [1] For example: On the role of the carbon cycle in photosynthesis, teacher assesses whether students comprehend the counter-intuitive concept that a gas (carbon dioxide) contributes most of the mass to the plants structure. Students look at a picture of a giant sequoia tree and answer the question: “Where did most of the matter that makes up the wood and the leaves of this huge tree originally come from?” Students circle the best answer in a multiple-choice question and explain their thinking. [1] This additional phase of the learning cycle could allow teachers to assure that students understand the science conceptually.

Citations [1] E. Duran, L. Duran, J. Haney, and A. Scheurmann. A Learning Cycle for All Students. The Science Teacher, 78(3):56-60, 2011. [2] P.G. Hewitt. Conceptual Physics-Turning Nonscience Students on to Their Everyday Environments. Physics Teacher, 10(9):515-522, 1972.
